title: Investigate: GET /api/portfolio's first load is very slow; can IBKR speed it up when connected?
description:
User-reported performance issue: the Portfolio page's first load is 'very very slow'. Investigated the current implementation before writing this task (read, not profiled live -- this task's first job is to actually measure, not assume):

`GET /api/portfolio` (`get_portfolio` in `app/api/routers/portfolio.py`) currently does, for a portfolio of N held positions in swing mode (the default, and almost certainly what the reporting user has active): (1) `enrich_positions_with_price` fetches each position's current price via the swing `DataProvider` (yfinance-primary/Stooq-fallback behind a SQLite cache) -- whether this loop is sequential or already concurrent needs checking directly, not assumed; (2) a separate `for e in enriched` loop then calls `_compute_position_signal`, which for EVERY position in swing mode makes ANOTHER blocking `provider.get_weekly_ohlcv(ticker)` call, sequentially, one position at a time, with no concurrency at all. So a swing-mode portfolio load can be up to ~2N sequential external-provider round trips (cache-cold ones going all the way to a real yfinance/Stooq HTTP request), a plausible root cause for 'very very slow' -- but this needs to be *confirmed* by actually timing it (e.g. add temporary instrumentation, or profile with `cProfile`/manual timestamps around the two loops) before assuming this is the whole story rather than something else (DB query patterns, template config, etc.).

Day-trader mode already has a fully-worked-out concurrent-fetch pattern for exactly this N-tickers problem (`compute_day_trader_signals_concurrently`, `ThreadPoolExecutor`-based, from `backend-day-trader-timeframe-mode-api-followups`) -- that pattern is a strong, low-risk template for speeding up the SWING-mode loops above too, independent of whether IBKR is involved at all (concurrent fetching from the existing swing `DataProvider` itself, no new data source).

The user's own specific ask -- 'can it be faster when using ibkr as much as possible if ibkr is connected' -- is a genuinely bigger, more architecturally sensitive question: it implies substituting or supplementing the swing-mode price/weekly-data fetch with IBKR when available. This directly touches an already-established precedent recorded elsewhere in this codebase's task history: `current_price`/`equity` are documented as 'always swing-provider-derived regardless of the active trading mode' (see `PortfolioResponse.trading_mode`'s own field description and prior day-trader-mode API decisions). Changing that for swing mode specifically -- even only 'when IBKR happens to be connected' -- is a real product/architecture decision, not a pure performance optimization, since it would mean two different portfolios (same account, different moments) could show prices sourced from two different providers depending on IBKR's connection state. This task should investigate whether IBKR even CAN supply what's needed here (IBKR's `IBKRProvider` today only exposes hourly bars/scanner/account-positions -- not a documented daily/weekly OHLCV fetch matching the swing provider's shape) and, if so, treat the swing-vs-IBKR-source question as something to resolve via a `decisions` entry with real weighing of the tradeoff, or escalate as a `questions` entry (state: waiting_input) if it's genuinely the user's call to make -- do not silently start mixing data sources into swing mode's price fields without that explicit resolution.

checklist.step: Measure, don't assume: instrument (or profile) `GET /api/portfolio` against a portfolio with several held positions and a cold cache, and identify where the actual wall-clock time goes -- confirm or correct the hypothesis above (the `enrich_positions_with_price` fetch loop and/or `_compute_position_signal`'s per-position `get_weekly_ohlcv` loop being sequential and provider-round-trip-bound).

If the sequential swing-provider loops are confirmed as the bottleneck: apply concurrent fetching to them, following the same `ThreadPoolExecutor`-based pattern `compute_day_trader_signals_concurrently` already established for the analogous day-trader-mode problem -- this is independent of IBKR and should be safe/low-risk to do regardless of the answer to the IBKR question below. Verify thread-safety against the swing `DataProvider`'s actual implementation (mirroring how the day-trader concurrency work verified `IBKRProvider`'s own mutable-state usage) before assuming it's safe.

Separately investigate whether IBKR can genuinely supply what swing mode's price/weekly-data fetch needs today (check `IBKRProvider`'s actual current capabilities -- hourly bars, account positions, scanner -- against what a daily/weekly-OHLCV-shaped fetch would require) -- if it can't without new IBKR-provider work, say so explicitly and treat that as this task's answer to the user's question (a follow-up task, not silently expanded scope here) rather than attempting a larger IBKR-provider feature under an 'investigation' task's checklist.

If IBKR genuinely could supply swing-mode data faster when connected: record the swing-vs-IBKR-source tradeoff as a `decisions` entry (or a `questions` entry + `waiting_input` state if it's genuinely the user's call, given the precedent tension described in this task's own description) BEFORE implementing anything that changes what `current_price`/`equity`/signal inputs are sourced from in swing mode -- do not silently change this established behavior.

Tests: for whatever concurrency change is made, a genuinely discriminating test proving the concurrent fetch produces the same per-position results as the old sequential loop (not just 'doesn't crash') -- mutation-test it per this codebase's established standard for concurrency-correctness claims.

decisions.decision: Confirmed the hypothesis via an ad hoc timing script (TestClient + a `DataProvider` stand-in that sleeps 0.05s per call to simulate a real yfinance/Stooq round trip, N held positions, cold cache): for N=10 positions in swing mode, GET /api/portfolio issued exactly 10 `get_daily_ohlcv` + 10 `get_weekly_ohlcv` calls (2N as hypothesized), fully sequentially, for a measured ~1.31s wall-clock time against a fully-sequential-equivalent of 1.00s (20 * 0.05s) plus request/signal-computation overhead. Confirmed `enrich_positions_with_price` was NOT already concurrent (contrary to the description's uncertainty on this point) and `_compute_position_signal`'s per-position `get_weekly_ohlcv` call was also fully sequential -- both loops are genuinely the bottleneck the description hypothesized, not something else (DB query patterns were already 1-query-per-table thanks to prior N+1 fixes; template/serialization overhead is negligible next to 20 real network-bound calls). No DB-query-pattern or other alternative cause was found to compete with this as the dominant cost.
decisions.rationale: The task's own checklist requires measuring rather than assuming. A sleep-based stand-in provider is the standard way this codebase already reproduces 'slow external I/O' in a test/profiling context without a live network call (matches Testing.md's no-live-network-calls rule) -- rejected alternatives: (1) cProfile against the real yfinance provider, which would require live network access this sandboxed environment doesn't have and would violate the no-live-network-call testing convention if committed as a test; (2) trusting the code-read-only hypothesis in the task's own description without measuring it, which the checklist explicitly forbids.

decisions.decision: Applied ThreadPoolExecutor-based concurrent fetching to both confirmed-sequential loops: (1) `app.portfolio.pricing.enrich_positions_with_price` now fans its per-row `latest_close` calls out across a small thread pool (`_MAX_CONCURRENT_PRICE_FETCHES = 8`, same value as `app.api.day_trader_signal._MAX_CONCURRENT_TICKER_FETCHES`) instead of looping sequentially; (2) a new `app.api.routers.portfolio._prefetch_swing_weekly_ohlcv` fetches every swing-mode position's `get_weekly_ohlcv` concurrently up front (mirroring `compute_day_trader_signals_concurrently`'s existing prefetch-then-lookup shape for day-trader mode), and `_compute_position_signal` now looks the result up from that prefetched dict instead of fetching inline. Re-measured with the same timing script after the change: N=10 dropped from ~1.31s to ~0.51s wall-clock (a ~61% reduction), and N=30 dropped from a ~3.0s fully-sequential-equivalent to ~1.2s (~2.5x), both consistent with the 8-worker-pool bound (ceil(N/8) round trips per phase instead of N). Verified thread-safety against the real `CachedDataProvider` (app/data/cache.py) specifically: its own docstring and `self._lock` were already established (by the backend-indicator-history-performance task's concurrent daily+weekly fetch in `get_indicator_history`) to serialize every DB-touching section of its public methods while leaving only the actual network fetch unlocked -- the same precondition this task's new concurrent fetches rely on, so no new thread-safety work was needed in `CachedDataProvider` itself. Also updated `tests/integration/test_portfolio_pricing_session.py`'s own hand-rolled in-memory-SQLite engine to use `StaticPool` (previously bare `check_same_thread=False`): once `enrich_positions_with_price` itself spins up worker threads, that test's session is genuinely touched from more than one OS thread, and a `:memory:` SQLite engine without `StaticPool` hands a different (empty) database to a different thread -- the same reason `tests/integration/conftest.py`'s own shared `db_session` fixture already needed `StaticPool` for `TestClient`'s request-handling thread.
decisions.rationale: The task's checklist explicitly directs following `compute_day_trader_signals_concurrently`'s established ThreadPoolExecutor pattern rather than inventing a different concurrency mechanism (asyncio, multiprocessing), and directs verifying thread-safety against the real provider's implementation rather than assuming it. `GET /api/portfolio/risk` (`get_risk`) has an analogous sequential `provider.get_weekly_ohlcv` call in its own swing-mode first-pass loop, but was deliberately NOT touched by this task: that loop interleaves a cheap, no-network filter (`_stop_and_filtered_daily`/`protective_stop`) with the weekly fetch specifically so a position that fails the cheap check never pays for a weekly round trip that would be thrown away -- naively prefetching weekly data for every swing position up front (the same shape as this task's `_prefetch_swing_weekly_ohlcv`) would defeat that existing optimization for positions that would have been filtered out first. `get_risk` still benefits from this task's other fix (it calls the now-concurrent `enrich_positions_with_price` too), and its own weekly-fetch loop wasn't part of this task's measured hypothesis/checklist scope (which named `GET /api/portfolio` specifically) -- fixing it properly would need its own two-phase (cheap-filter-then-concurrent-fetch-the-survivors) design, left as a candidate for the `backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups` task created alongside this one rather than expanding this task's own scope. `_prefetch_swing_weekly_ohlcv` was implemented as its own small local ThreadPoolExecutor helper in `app/api/routers/portfolio.py`, NOT by reusing `app.api.day_trader_signal`'s private `_fan_out_per_ticker` (even though this module already imports several other names from that module): `day_trader_signal.py`'s own module docstring scopes it to day-trader-mode IBKR orchestration specifically, and its `_fan_out_per_ticker` helper is a private, non-exported implementation detail of that scope -- reusing it for an unrelated swing-mode concern would couple two independently-evolving features through a private symbol never intended as a shared API. Likewise, `enrich_positions_with_price`'s own concurrency was implemented directly in `app/portfolio/pricing.py` (not by importing anything from `app/api/day_trader_signal.py`) because `docs/architecture/Backend.md` documents `app/portfolio/pricing.py` as depending only on `app/data/base.py`/`app/data/exceptions.py`/`app/db/models.py`/`app/portfolio/models.py` and being 'imported only from the api/ layer' -- importing an api-layer module from it would invert that documented dependency direction. Both new helpers duplicate the small ThreadPoolExecutor-fan-out shape rather than share one utility function, since the two call sites live in different architectural layers (`app/portfolio/` vs `app/api/routers/`) with no existing shared lower-layer module for exactly this kind of generic concurrency helper to live in -- judged not worth introducing a new shared module for ~15 lines of straightforward stdlib usage duplicated twice, but noted here as a discretionary tradeoff a reviewer may reasonably weigh differently.

decisions.decision: Confirmed `IBKRProvider` (app/data/ibkr_provider.py) cannot supply a daily/weekly-OHLCV-shaped fetch matching the swing `DataProvider` protocol today: its only market-data method is `get_hourly_bars` (paginated `/iserver/marketdata/history` calls, native granularity is intraday -- `'1h'` default, other IBKR-documented bar sizes down to minutes -- with a 20-page pagination safety bound sized against `'1h'` bars, ~833 days of history), plus `get_scanner_params`/`run_scanner` (market scanner, unrelated) and `get_account_positions` (account holdings, unrelated). There is no native daily or weekly bar endpoint wired up, and no existing resample-hourly-to-daily/weekly pipeline for it (the closest precedent, `app.data.day_trader_intraday`'s own intraday-bar resampling via `app.data.base.resample_ohlcv`, only ever targets day-trader-mode's own short intraday windows, not a full swing-shaped multi-year daily/weekly history). Building that resampling pipeline would also inherit `get_hourly_bars`' own ~833-day lookback ceiling, which is far short of what swing mode's weekly-EMA/MACD seeding needs (`YFinanceProvider._MIN_WEEKLY_BARS = 26` weekly bars is the hard floor, but `analyse()`'s own Screen 1/Tide and other indicators read considerably more history than that in practice) -- so even a resampling pipeline wouldn't be a drop-in equivalent to the yfinance/Stooq daily/weekly fetch without also solving a materially shorter available-history window. This is genuine new IBKR-provider feature work (a new fetch method, a resampling adapter, and a decision on how to handle the shorter history window), not something achievable within this investigation task's own checklist scope.
decisions.rationale: The task's own checklist explicitly directs treating a 'no, not without new IBKR-provider work' finding as the answer to the user's underlying question, via a follow-up task, rather than attempting the larger feature here. This mirrors `backend-day-trader-timeframe-mode-api`'s own precedent of scoping day-trader-mode support down to fully-`MINUTE`-unit triples only, rather than building a new fetch pipeline for a mixed/daily/weekly triple leg IBKR has no established path for.

decisions.decision: Because checklist item 3 found IBKR genuinely CANNOT supply swing-mode's price/weekly-data fetch today without new provider work, checklist item 4's premise ('if IBKR genuinely could supply swing-mode data faster when connected') does not currently hold -- so no change was made to `current_price`/`equity`/signal-input sourcing in swing mode, and the established 'always swing-provider-derived regardless of trading mode' precedent (`PortfolioResponse.trading_mode`'s own field description) is left completely untouched by this task. This is recorded as a `decisions` entry (not escalated to a `questions`/`waiting_input` entry) because the investigation itself resolved the question -- there is no genuine tradeoff for a human to weigh yet, since the IBKR-side capability that tradeoff would depend on doesn't exist. Filed `docs/tasks/backend-portfolio-load-performance-followups.json` (depends_on this task) to track the larger 'build an IBKR-backed daily/weekly-shaped fetch and then decide the swing-vs-IBKR-source tradeoff' work as a distinct, explicitly-scoped follow-up rather than silently expanding this investigation task -- that follow-up task's own checklist re-poses the swing-vs-IBKR precedent-tension question (a `decisions` entry or `questions`/`waiting_input` escalation, per this task's original description) for whoever picks it up once/if that IBKR capability is built.
decisions.rationale: Per this task's checklist item 3's own wording, a 'can't without new work' finding is itself the answer, to be handled via a follow-up task rather than by asking the user a hypothetical question about a capability that doesn't exist yet ('would you want IBKR prices when it can't currently provide them?' has no useful answer to give right now). Escalating this as a `questions`/`waiting_input` entry instead would stall this otherwise-complete, already-measured-and-fixed performance task on a question that can't actually be answered meaningfully today -- the follow-up task is the more honest place to raise it once the underlying capability question (build the IBKR daily/weekly fetch, or don't) is itself resolved.

decisions.decision: Added genuinely discriminating regression tests for both new concurrent fetches, and manually mutation-tested each before finalizing: `tests/unit/test_portfolio_pricing.py::TestEnrichPositionsWithPrice::test_result_order_matches_row_order_even_when_completion_order_differs` and `tests/integration/test_portfolio_get.py::TestGetPortfolioSignal::test_weekly_prefetch_outcome_not_swapped_when_completion_order_differs_from_submission_order` each use a per-ticker-configurable-delay stand-in provider where the FIRST-submitted ticker is deliberately the SLOWEST to complete (and fails), while the second-submitted ticker finishes first (and succeeds) -- a same-latency fixture couldn't distinguish 'results correctly keyed by ticker/submission order' from 'results accidentally keyed by completion order' (e.g. via `as_completed(...)` instead of iterating the originally-submitted futures/dict in order), since both orderings would coincidentally agree when every fetch takes the same amount of time. Manually verified each test's discriminating power by temporarily mutating the corresponding implementation to introduce exactly that completion-order bug (`as_completed` in place of iterating `futures`/`futures.items()` in submission order) and confirming the new test failed, then reverted the mutation and reran the full suite (1454 passed) to confirm a clean baseline.
decisions.rationale: This codebase's established standard for concurrency-correctness claims (`app.api.day_trader_signal`'s own `TestComputeDayTraderSignalsConcurrently::test_maps_each_distinct_ticker_to_its_own_outcome_not_a_shared_or_swapped_one`) requires a test that would actually fail under a plausible per-ticker-result-mixup bug, not merely a 'runs without crashing' smoke test with same-shaped-but-not-genuinely-distinguishing fixtures. A same-latency multi-ticker fixture (e.g. this codebase's existing `test_multiple_positions_are_all_enriched`) already catches a naive value-swap bug (since positions are asserted by ticker), but wouldn't catch a completion-order-vs-submission-order bug specifically -- deliberately mismatched per-ticker latency was needed to force that distinction to actually matter.
